# a2a-js: the official JavaScript SDK for the Agent2Agent protocol

Official JavaScript SDK for the Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol

647 stars 179 forks TypeScript Apache-2.0

GitHub Official website

## At a glance

What is it?
    @a2a-js/sdk is the official TypeScript and JavaScript SDK for the A2A protocol, giving you one DefaultRequestHandler behind three wire transports, an opt-in compatibility layer for v0.3 peers, and persistent task stores with a migrations CLI. It suits teams building agent servers or clients in Node, and it commits you to the A2A message and task model rather than letting you invent one.

Who is it for?
    a2a-js is the right choice if you are building an A2A server or client in Node and want the protocol surface, the task lifecycle and the transport bindings handled by the official implementation rather than by hand. It is the wrong choice for a browser-only agent, since the gRPC transport is Node-only and the package requires Node 20 or newer, and it is the wrong choice if your peers are still firmly on v0.3 and you would rather wait for the compatibility layer to stabilise.

Can I use it commercially?
    Yes. Apache-2.0 is a permissive licence: you can use, modify and sell software built on it, as long as you keep its copyright and licence notices.

Is it still maintained?
    Yes. The repository received new commits within the last day.

What is it written in?
    Mainly TypeScript, according to GitHub's language statistics.

Answers come from the project's GitHub data, last synced on October 23, 2026, and from our analysis. They are not legal advice.

## Editorial analysis

Reviewed and approved by Eden on October 22, 2026. Last updated October 22, 2026. 7 min read

ContentsInstalling the SDK and choosing a transportSubpath exports and where each piece livesThe v0.3 compatibility layer is opt in, and that is the pointTask lifecycle, cancellation and push notifications in the samplesPersistent stores and the a2a-db migration CLIInterceptors, the interactive CLI and the project layout


The package is organised entirely through subpath exports, and the typesVersions map in the manifest shows the full surface: errors, errors/grpc, server, server/express, server/grpc, server/database, client, client/grpc, and six compat/v0_3 entries covering the base, server, express, grpc, client and client/grpc variants.

That layout is informative because it tells you the dependency direction. The core errors module is separate from the gRPC error helpers, so code that only handles protocol errors does not pull in the gRPC stack. The database entry point is separate from the server entry point, which means persistence is opt in at the import level rather than something a server picks up by default. The compat entries mirror the main layout exactly, which is what a compatibility layer that has to sit underneath every transport tends to look like.

The server/database and server/express subpaths also explain the install instructions. Using the Express integration means importing from @a2a-js/sdk/server/express, and since Express is a peer dependency rather than a bundled one, you install it yourself. The same pattern applies to the gRPC transport with @grpc/grpc-js and @bufbuild/protobuf, and to persistent stores with Kysely plus a driver. Peer dependencies here are the right design for a library that has to work inside someone else's server, but it does mean the install step is a decision tree rather than one command.

### Editorial conclusion

a2a-js is the right choice if you are building an A2A server or client in Node and want the protocol surface, the task lifecycle and the transport bindings handled by the official implementation rather than by hand. It is the wrong choice for a browser-only agent, since the gRPC transport is Node-only and the package requires Node 20 or newer, and it is the wrong choice if your peers are still firmly on v0.3 and you would rather wait for the compatibility layer to stabilise. Before adopting it, read the migration guide if you are coming from 0.3.x, confirm your persistence needs by running the a2a-db CLI migrations against a real database rather than assuming the SQLite default, and check that the spec version your peers speak matches the v1.0.0 surface this SDK implements.

### Frequently asked questions

#### How do I install the A2A JavaScript SDK?

Run npm install @a2a-js/sdk. Peer dependencies are extra: npm install express for the Express integration, npm install @grpc/grpc-js @bufbuild/protobuf for the gRPC transport, and npm install kysely with a driver for persistent stores.

#### Which transports does @a2a-js/sdk support?

Three: JSON-RPC, HTTP+JSON/REST and gRPC, each with both a client and a server implementation, all backed by a single DefaultRequestHandler. The gRPC transport is Node.js only.

#### Can an a2a-js server talk to a peer still on A2A v0.3?

Yes, through an opt-in v0.3 compatibility layer. The compat-v1-server sample enables legacyCompat on every transport, and a separate v0.3 compatibility guide is published under docs/.

#### What databases can I use for persistent tasks in @a2a-js/sdk?

PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and Cloudflare D1 are supported through Kysely, with an a2a-db CLI for migrations. The driver is a peer dependency you install yourself, for example pg, mysql2, better-sqlite3 or kysely-d1.

#### What licence is the A2A JavaScript SDK under?

Apache-2.0. The repository is not archived and the last push was on 2026-10-19, with v1.3.0 released on 2026-09-29, v1.2.1 on 2026-09-24 and v1.2.0 on 2026-09-18.

## Version negotiation is one header

The compatibility story rests on a single service parameter. Clients MUST send `A2A-Version` on every request, in `Major.Minor` form; patch numbers are explicitly excluded from negotiation. Agents MUST serve the requested semantics or return `VersionNotSupportedError`. Clients MAY pass it as a query parameter instead of a header, which matters for environments that mangle custom headers.

The default is the trap — an empty `A2A-Version` MUST be interpreted as 0.3, not as the newest version. A client that forgets the header does not fail loudly; it silently gets 0.3 semantics from any agent that still speaks it.

Because `protocolVersion` now lives per interface, one agent can advertise 0.3 and 1.0 side by side, on the same URL or different ones, and let the client pick. The Agent Card evolved in a backward-compatible way precisely so this dual advertisement is possible while the interaction protocol itself broke.

The SDKs implement this as an explicit compatibility layer rather than as best-effort tolerance. In the Python SDK, `src/a2a/utils/constants.py` defines `PROTOCOL_VERSION_1_0`, `PROTOCOL_VERSION_0_3` and `PROTOCOL_VERSION_CURRENT = PROTOCOL_VERSION_1_0`, and an entire `a2a/compat/v0_3/` package holds model conversions plus JSON-RPC and REST transports that stamp the 0.3 header on outbound calls. The JavaScript SDK mirrors it: `src/compat/v0_3/` dispatches on the header — requests whose version is not in `[0.3, 1.0)` are routed onward — and its Agent Card handler serves a version-specific ETag with `Vary: A2A-Version`.

That last detail is the one to copy. Version-negotiated content behind a CDN needs the `Vary` header or you will cache a 0.3 card and serve it to a 1.0 client.

SDK version numbers, meanwhile, do not track the protocol. At audit time the latest releases were a2a-python `v1.1.2` (2026-07-22), a2a-js `v1.0.1` (2026-07-28), a2a-java `v1.2.0.Final` (2026-08-07), a2a-go `v2.4.0` (2026-07-28) and a2a-dotnet `v1.0.0-preview2` (2026-04-09). Read the constants, not the tag.

## Talking to a remote agent

flotti speaks A2A through the official SDK, `@a2a-js/sdk`, so the protocol details — transports, the `A2A-Version` header, version 0.3 of the protocol — are the SDK's and not flotti's. In code it is `A2AAgent` (`src/a2a-agent.ts`), a `FleetAgent` like a local agent: the dashboard gets the same events and drives it the same way.

  * The card. It is read from `<url>/.well-known/agent-card.json`, or from `url` itself when that names a `.json` file. It is read once on connecting, not before every message: a card whose `Cache-Control` says it is fresh is not asked for at all, and after that it is asked for with `If-None-Match`. When the card offers an extended card, that one is read too.
  * Versions. Agents that speak A2A 1.0 and 0.3 both work; the dashboard shows which one is spoken. Of the transports, JSON-RPC and HTTP+JSON are used; gRPC is not.
  * Answers. An agent that can stream answers as it goes. One that cannot is asked for its task every two seconds until the task is done.

  * Clients MAY use `taskId` (with or without `contextId`) to continue or refine a specific task
  * Clients MAY use `contextId` without `taskId` to start a new task within an existing conversation context
  * Agents MUST infer `contextId` from the task if only `taskId` is provided
  * Agents MUST reject messages containing mismatching `contextId` and `taskId` (i.e., the provided `contextId` is different from that of the referenced `Task`).

Input Required State:

  * Agents can request additional input mid-processing by transitioning a task to the `input-required` state
  * The client continues the interaction by sending a new message with the same `taskId` and `contextId`

Follow-up Messages:

  * Clients can send additional messages with `taskId` references to continue or refine existing tasks
  * Clients SHOULD use the `referenceTaskIds` field in `Message` to explicitly reference related tasks
  * Agents SHOULD use referenced tasks to understand the context and intent of follow-up requests

Context Inheritance:

  * New tasks created within the same `contextId` can inherit context from previous interactions
  * Agents SHOULD leverage the shared `contextId` to provide contextually relevant responses

The method field carries the operation name (for example, `message/send` or `tasks/get`). Responses follow JSON-RPC 2.0 conventions for both success and error cases.^{[4]}

Clients indicate the protocol version they expect using the `A2A-Version` header. Servers must process requests per the indicated version semantics or return a `VersionNotSupportedError`. Supported protocol bindings are declared in the Agent Card's `preferredTransport` and `additionalInterfaces` fields. As of version 1.0, each binding may declare its own version number, allowing servers to roll forward the JSON-RPC interface while keeping gRPC or REST at older revisions during migration windows.^{[8]}

### Streaming via server-sent events

Many agentic tasks take longer than a simple HTTP request-response cycle can accommodate. A2A supports real-time incremental result delivery through server-sent events over a persistent HTTP connection. The `SendStreamingMessage` operation opens such a connection. The server then emits `TaskStatusUpdateEvent` objects as the task state changes and `TaskArtifactUpdateEvent` objects as partial outputs become available.

Its “What’s New in v1.0” page has a section called “Breaking Changes Requiring Code Updates”, marks Part type unification as “CRITICAL IMPACT”, and rates the stream-event discriminator, the agent-card structure, changed enum values and standardised errors via `google.rpc.Status` as “HIGH IMPACT” and pagination as “MEDIUM IMPACT”. It adds agent-card signing with JSON Web Signatures, and a version header: clients send `A2A-Version`, and a server that does not support the requested version returns an error listing what it does support. We did not test any of this against a running agent.

## Which protocols does A2A run over?

Three. The specification has a section for each: “JSON-RPC Protocol Binding”, “gRPC Protocol Binding” and “HTTP+JSON/REST Protocol Binding”, and says the protocol “supports multiple protocol bindings”, with a section on functional equivalence between them. Google’s AI Overview lists “HTTP(S), JSON-RPC 2.0, Server-Sent Events (SSE), and JSON”. The word gRPC appears 47 times in the specification and not once in the Overview, which also does not name the REST binding. For security, the specification mentions OAuth 44 times, OpenID 3 times, mTLS once and JSON Web Signature 5 times, which is consistent with the Overview’s “TLS, JWTs, and OpenID Connect” but not the whole picture.

## Who governs A2A now?

The Agentic AI Foundation. Its announcement, dated 27 August 2026, says A2A “has officially been accepted as a Growth Stage project at the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF)”, operating “under the Linux Foundation-directed AAIF alongside sibling projects like MCP, goose, and AGENTS.md”. The specification site’s footer reads “Copyright 2026 The Linux Foundation”. Google’s AI Overview says A2A is “governed by the Linux Foundation”, which is accurate but does not mention the foundation or that MCP is a sibling project. The announcement also says the protocol is “backed by over 150 organizations”, which is the project’s own figure and we did not verify it.
